details: Spatially Balanced Sampling through the Pivotal Method. Biometrics 68(2), 514-520. DOI 10.1111/j.1541-0420.2011.01699.x. Online date 2011-10-31, so the year is 2011 online and 2012 in print. Abstract: a simple method for spatially balanced samples with equal or unequal inclusion probabilities, working in any number of dimensions including spaces defined by several auxiliary variables; the authors report high spatial balance and efficiency for populations with trends. Source: Crossref record.
bears_on: C8 (a randomized spread-out selection that has known inclusion probabilities, in contrast to greedy k-center); C6 (selection on auxiliary variables). The abstract does not give a variance estimator [verify].

details: Functional central limit theorems for single-stage sampling designs. Annals of Statistics 45(4), 1728-1758 per Crossref (DOI 10.1214/16-AOS1507). Abstract: functional CLTs for Horvitz-Thompson and Hajek empirical processes, for model-based and design-based inference, with conditions mainly on higher-order correlations, applied to Hadamard differentiable functionals. The companion paper Boistard, Lopuhaa, Ruiz-Gazen 2012 (EJS 6, 1967-1983, arXiv 1207.5654) approximates rejective sampling joint inclusion probabilities and supplies the high-order correlation bounds.
bears_on: C5 and C7 (asymptotic normality of HT and Hajek estimators under rejective sampling, as a large-population result); not a few-cluster result.

details: Only one single-author Chauvet 2012 item was found: On a characterization of ordered pivotal sampling, Bernoulli 18(4), 1320-1340, DOI 10.3150/11-BEJ380 (arXiv 1211.5442). It shows ordered pivotal sampling equals Deville's systematic sampling, which gives second-order inclusion probabilities, and that a good ordering can lower variance. It is not an asymptotics paper. The pivotal-sampling asymptotics paper found is Chauvet, Martingale central-limit theorems for pivotal sampling, arXiv 1510.08895 (2015). Which one the seed meant is unconfirmed [verify].
bears_on: C6 (pair probabilities for pivotal sampling are exact and need no simulation); C7.

details: An adaptive algorithm for estimating inclusion probabilities and performing the Horvitz-Thompson criterion in complex designs. Computational Statistics 24(4), 623-639. DOI 10.1007/s00180-009-0149-9. Published online 2009-03-28. Abstract not read [verify]. Source: Crossref record (title and bibliographic data only).
bears_on: C6 and C7 (simulation-based estimation of first-order and joint inclusion probabilities, follow-up to Fattorini 2006).

details: Simulation-based randomized systematic PPS sampling under substitution of units. Survey Methodology, 2008 issue 1, article 12-001-X200800110613 (volume 34 [verify], pages not shown on page). Abstract: upper-level clusters selected by randomized systematic PPS, with substitutes drawn when selected clusters refuse; first-order inclusion probabilities become hard and second-order nearly intractable; a simulation-based method estimates both; theory, numerical examples and R/S-PLUS code given. Earlier version in Statistics Canada Symposium 2006 (11-522-X200600110424). The title found differs from the brief's wording (estimation of second-order inclusion probabilities) but the content matches.
bears_on: C6 and C7 (cluster-level simulated first- and second-order inclusion probabilities in a design-based analysis).

details: Asymptotic theory of rejective sampling with varying probabilities from a finite population. Annals of Mathematical Statistics 35(4), 1491-1523 (MR0178555), confirmed from the reference list of Sen (1995, Kybernetika 31(3), 251-268). Rejective sampling is Poisson sampling conditioned on the sample size, that is conditional Poisson sampling [from memory, not read this session]. The Project Euclid page could not be read (bot protection), and the Crossref lookup was rate limited. Abstract not read.
bears_on: C5 and C7 (rejective sampling terminology and joint inclusion probability expansions; Boistard et al. 2012 extend it).

details: On the two different aspects of the representative method: the method of stratified sampling and the method of purposive selection. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society 97(4), 558-625. Full text read at https://errorstatistics.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/neyman-1934.pdf. Districts chosen so a weighted mean of a control variable matches the population value (Bowley, Gini and Galvani). Neyman treats this as a non-random special case of stratified sampling, states there is no room for probabilities or standard errors without random selection, and notes the estimator is consistent only under a linearity hypothesis that cannot be tested. With few large districts most strata hold zero or one district.
bears_on: C8 (historical statement that purposive selection of a few groups yields no design-based standard error); also C5 and C6 as the case for randomization within balance.

details: Two papers, usually cited as Robust estimation in finite populations I and II, Journal of the American Statistical Association 68 (volume per the brief; titles and pages not confirmed this session [verify]). The Crossref lookup was rate limited. Described in Brewer, Three controversies in the history of survey sampling (Survey Methodology 39(2), 2013): Royall suggested a balanced sample, meaning sample moments of x as close as possible to population moments, a purposive design evaluated under the prediction model.
bears_on: C5, C6 and C8 (balanced purposive selection justified by a model, with variance defined under the model, not the design).

details: An Evaluation of Model-Dependent and Probability-Sampling Inferences in Sample Surveys. Journal of the American Statistical Association (title confirmed from Valliant's Hansen lecture; the volume is 78 per the brief; pages not confirmed [verify]). Described in the sources read as a simulation showing a small model misspecification can cause important bias in a model-based estimator under an ignorable design with full response. Brewer notes the design-based side did not point out that balance would protect against it.
bears_on: C8 and C6 (design-based inference as protection against model failure; the case for random selection even with balance).

details: Penalized balanced sampling. Biometrika 99(4), 945-958. DOI 10.1093/biomet/ass033. Published online 2012-07-26. Abstract: uses linear mixed models at the design stage, reviews balanced sampling and the cube algorithm, proposes a cube implementation that selects penalized balanced samples; Horvitz-Thompson estimators from such samples are highly efficient when a linear mixed model in the auxiliary variables fits; Monte Carlo experiments with nonparametric and temporal mixed models. The companion Breidt and Chauvet (2011), improved variance estimation for balanced samples drawn via the cube method, was searched for (Q13) but not located or verified.
bears_on: C6 (balancing on a fitted score or smoother using the cube method and design-based Horvitz-Thompson analysis).
